title: Why Financial Literacy Should Grow With Students, From High School to College

- Why Financial Literacy Should Grow With Students, From High School to College


Financial literacy courses have become an increasingly common graduation requirement in US high schools. But can a single course prepare students for the financial demands of early adulthood and beyond? The recent[Evaluating FinFutures](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/406090471_Evaluating_FinFutures_Budgeting_Confidence_and_Capability_in_First_Year_Experience) study by Intuit for Education (I4E) and DIA Higher Education Collaborators suggests that students benefit greatly from ongoing financial learning.


Researchers found that most students recognized the value of budgeting, but far fewer felt confident doing it. While courses are certainly a step in the right direction, they appear to function better as a foundation than a finish line.


## Key Points


- 60% of college students said budgeting was important, but fewer than half felt confident creating one, according to the *Evaluating FinFutures* study by Intuit for Education (I4E) and DIA Higher Education Collaborators.
- The share of students reporting high confidence in their ability to create a budget increased from 40.4% before FinFutures to 59.4% afterward.
- Students improved by similar margins after completing FinFutures, regardless of their financial education history.
- Developed by I4E, FinFutures combines a budgeting simulation and lesson plan with curricular content and self-assessments.
- Respondents who had completed a financial literacy course generally went into the study with more budgeting confidence but similar levels of financial worry.


## The Gap Between Financial Knowledge and Financial Readiness


The transition from high school to college is often exciting and stressful. Many young adults live independently for the first time but have limited resources and little time available for work. Managing everyday expenses alongside college costs can be a challenge.


According to the *Evaluating FinFutures* study, students generally recognized that budgeting mattered. 60% met the study’s proficiency threshold for value beliefs, but only 43% were actively budgeting.


Additionally, just under half felt confident enough in their skills to meet the confidence benchmark. When asked specifically about creating a realistic budget, only 25% of students selected one of the top two confidence categories.


That gap between attitude and action existed alongside real financial pressure. Nearly 7 in 10 students reported worry levels consistent with significant concern in at least two areas:


- Worrying about paying for college (33%)
- Worrying about having enough money for necessities (29%)
- Worrying about running out of money (42%)
- Worrying about transportation to and from school (13%)
- Worrying about affording materials for classes (24%)


The question is whether financial education can close this gap. The prevalence of financial literacy courses in high schools has been on the rise, with 39 states now requiring students to take a personal finance course to graduate, according to the[Council for Economic Education (CEE)](https://www.councilforeconed.org/survey-of-the-states/) .


In the *Evaluating FinFutures* study, about half of the respondents had completed a prior financial literacy course. Those students entered with significantly higher scores on budgeting confidence, behavioral intentions, and financial knowledge.


But prior coursework didn’t translate to less financial stress. Students who had taken a course averaged 3.16 on the study’s financial worry scale, compared with 3.25 among students who hadn’t—a difference that was not statistically significant. First-generation[college students](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/financial-literacy-college-students/) reported significantly higher financial worry than their continuing-generation peers, even though their confidence and motivation levels were comparable.

This suggests that while[high school financial literacy courses](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/financial-literacy-teens-young-adults/) may provide students with valuable knowledge, they don’t fully prepare students for the financial realities of college. Further,[college students](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/financial-tips/financial-literacy-college-students/) may benefit from continuing financial education as they begin navigating real-world responsibilities.


## What the Research Measured


I4E and DIA Higher Education Collaborators joined forces to investigate the impact of Intuit’s free financial literacy curriculum, FinFutures, on students at four post-secondary institutions. The study began with a pre-test survey to assess a variety of measures, including:


- Budgeting confidence (how capable students felt)
- Value beliefs (whether they thought budgeting mattered)
- Financial knowledge
- Financial worry
- Behavioral intentions (whether they planned to budget)
- Current budgeting behaviors


After the pre-test, participating students completed the FinFutures program, which includes a budgeting simulation and lesson plan, along with curricular content and self-assessments. A post-test followed to assess student reactions to the simulation experience, along with their post-simulation budgeting confidence, value beliefs, and behavioral intentions.


The final analysis included 765 pre-test responses and 389 post-survey responses.

## Students Benefited Similarly from FinFutures, Regardless of Previous Knowledge


Although completing a financial literacy course before the FinFutures test didn’t ease financial worry among college students in the study, it was associated with significantly higher scores on budgeting confidence, behavioral intentions, and value beliefs. Students who had taken a previous financial literacy course generally entered the experiment with a higher baseline.


**Financial Knowledge*** 0.56 (0.20) 0.53 (0.19) 4.60(1, 762) .032 .006


**Budgeting Confidence*** 3.54 (0.92) 3.29 (0.90) 14.60(1, 762) < .001 .019


**Behavioral Intention*** 3.46 (0.98) 3.24 (0.97) 9.69(1, 759) .002 .013


**Financial Worry** 3.16 (1.39) 3.25 (1.44) 0.71(1, 762) .399 .001


**Value Beliefs*** 3.78 (0.92) 3.62 (0.93) 6.25(1, 762) .013 .008


In reviewing the post-test results, students with prior course experience again scored higher on budgeting confidence, behavioral intention, and value beliefs. But in terms of how much each group improved from pre- to post-test, there were no statistically significant differences. Students improved by similar amounts regardless of whether they had previously completed a financial literacy course.

These findings suggest FinFutures still offers meaningful value to students who already have some financial literacy under their belt. But prior coursework doesn’t appear to be a prerequisite. Students without it saw similar gains in the study.


## Where Hands-On Practice Moved the Needle


FinFutures takes a unique approach to[teaching financial literacy](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/teaching-financial-literacy/) . Instead of relying on a traditional curriculum alone, the program features a budgeting simulation that puts students in realistic college financial scenarios. Students are asked to manage income, for example, working through expenses and making trade-off decisions. The program also gives them a budgeting template and walks students through creating their own budgets.


The program’s goal is to help students build applied skills through experiences that mirror real-life financial decisions, rather than just teaching financial concepts.


The early results are promising. Students in the I4E and DIA study showed gains in budgeting confidence, beliefs about the value of budgeting, and their intent to do it. And the share of students who reported high confidence in creating a budget rose from 40.4% before FinFutures to 59.4% afterward.


**Figure 2.** Pre and Post-FinFutures competency rates.


That suggests that hands-on practice may help bridge the gap between students knowing that a budget is important and feeling capable of managing one effectively.


## Building Financial Literacy That Lasts


Financial education looks different today than it did a generation ago. Personal finance wasn’t taught in many schools. And it wasn’t something families discussed openly. Today,[financial literacy courses](https://www.intuit.com/blog/global-stories/best-financial-literacy-courses/) are part of high school curricula in most states. And financial information is as accessible as ever through social media, AI tools, apps, and search engines. Yet the majority of college students still enter adulthood worried about their finances.


Intuit for Education is working to change that. Our free curriculum and tools give high school and college students a way to build[financial literacy](https://www.intuit.com/financial-literacy/) and confidence early. The platform pairs foundational lessons with real-world simulations, so students can put knowledge into practice.
